title: Ofsted Is Not the Enemy
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Responding to an NAHT survey showing that 52% of heads might quit after an inspection under England's new Ofsted framework, Salles argues that the stress comes less from the inspection than from how heads frame the judgement. He cites DfE figures showing that most schools meet the expected standard in every evaluation area, and reports from his wife, an inspector, that inspectors now go out of their way to be kind to heads after Ruth Perry's death. He treats special schools as a natural experiment: they are so oversubscribed that Ofsted has no effect on their survival, yet their heads are just as anxious, which suggests the pressure is largely self-imposed. His advice is to keep parents choosing your school through good progress and parent satisfaction, which makes the judgement irrelevant, and to use Parent View and progress data every year rather than waiting for inspectors. An analysis of Swindon schools suggests that parental views on SEND and behaviour track inspection findings far more closely than happiness or recommendation scores. Heads who release pressure and streamline work, he concludes, will actually do better.
points: Salles's claim is that head teacher stress is driven mainly by how heads frame the Ofsted judgement, not by adverse outcomes or hostile inspectors, since inspectors under the new framework are described as unusually attentive to head wellbeing.

Special schools act as a natural experiment: with near-guaranteed oversubscription Ofsted cannot threaten their survival, yet their heads report the same anxiety, which points to reputational fear as a self-imposed cause.
If parents keep choosing your school the judgement becomes irrelevant, and he argues that parents respond to progress results and to whether they feel the school values their child.

His Swindon Parent View analysis finds that parental satisfaction with SEND support, and with behaviour and bullying, aligns with Ofsted's criticisms, whereas happiness and recommendation rates do not predict the grade.

Leadership strengths Ofsted rewards are precise self-evaluation and good workload and professional development, so releasing pressure and streamlining work tends to improve both wellbeing and the judgement.
quotes: I’m going to argue that Ofsted is not responsible for this, and that the stres and pressure are actually of heads own making. I know that sounds unfair, so I am, as always, going to look for data.
Notice this stress is not because of an adverse judgement. Nor is it because of the attitude of the inspection team. It is because of the way heads frame the Ofsted judgement.
This is mind boggling. Would you rate other schools that highly? I very much doubt it. Ofsted is much kinder and more lenient than most teachers in your staffroom.

We have created a culture where Ofsted is a monster, and their judgement is the equivalent of a prison sentence or parole. The main cause of stress for a head teacher of a special school is mostly self imposed.
If you can keep parents choosing your school, the Ofsted judgement is irrelevant, just as it is in a special school.
You can ask your parents to complete Parent View every year. You don’t need to wait for Ofsted. You can look at your progress measures every year. You don’t need to wait for Ofsted.

What really matters to Ofsted is what your parents say about SEND. You probably feel a moral duty to make sure your SEND students succeed - and that is going to be your number one priority regarding Ofsted too.

If you are a head teacher experiencing the stress of Ofsted, you are most likely to ruin your judgement by adding more pressure and more work. But the opposite is also true - release the pressure, streamline the work, and you will actually get a better judgement.
You can only do that if you stop treating Ofsted as a monster. It isn’t. It is just a shadow under your bed.
context: Salles states his thesis up front: the pressure on heads is largely self-made, and he intends to test that with data.
He locates the source of stress in how heads interpret the judgement rather than in the result or the inspectors.
DfE grading data is used to argue that Ofsted is more lenient than heads imagine.
The special school natural experiment shows anxiety persisting where Ofsted has no real consequences.
Parent choice is his practical lever: a school that parents want is insulated from the judgement.
Heads can gather the same evidence Ofsted uses without waiting for an inspection.
The Swindon analysis points to SEND parent confidence as the factor that tracks inspection findings.
He ends with a counterintuitive prescription: less pressure and less work produce better outcomes.
The closing image reframes Ofsted as a shadow rather than a monster.
